DASS-21: Items and real responses

Source: R/data.R
dass.Rd

The 21 items of the short Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21; Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995), seven per scale, and the answers of 39,775 people who took the 42-item DASS online through the Open-Source Psychometrics Project from 2017 to 2019. The 21 items are taken from the 42 (the dass42 column says which). The DASS is public domain. Its structure is disputed, so it is a test case for the expected-structure checks (see sc_builtin_instrument()).

Usage

dass_items

dass_real

Format

dass_items: A data frame with 21 rows and 7 columns: item (DASS1 to DASS21, in DASS-21 order), scale (D, A or S), scale_label (Depression, Anxiety or Stress), statement, reverse (all FALSE), dass42 (the item in the 42-item DASS, for example Q22) and issue.

dass_real: A data frame with 39,775 rows and 24 columns: country (two-letter code from the respondent's network address, or NA; the largest groups are MY (21,605), US (8,207) and GB (1,180)), gender (factor), age (13 to 99, other entries NA) and the 21 items.

An object of class data.frame with 21 rows and 7 columns.

An object of class data.frame with 39775 rows and 24 columns.

Source

Open-Source Psychometrics Project, https://openpsychometrics.org/_rawdata/ (DASS data, 2019; only respondents who confirmed that their answers were accurate and could be used for research). The project gives no formal licence for the data. The DASS items are public domain (https://www2.psy.unsw.edu.au/dass/). The script is data-raw/instruments.R in the package's GitHub repository.

Details

Known problems. Whether the DASS-21 measures three distinct states is disputed: A bifactor model with a general distress factor often fits better than three correlated factors, and Stress overlaps with Anxiety (Henry & Crawford, 2005; Osman et al., 2012). The somatic anxiety items (dry mouth, breathing, trembling, heart rate) can reflect physical illness and often load weakly. In dass_real, item 2 ("I was aware of dryness of my mouth") has the lowest corrected item-total correlation within its scale (0.46; the others are 0.53 to 0.77). The issue column of dass_items gives a one-line note per item.

Answers are how much each statement applied over the past week, on a 4-point scale stored as given (1 = did not apply to me at all, 2 = to some degree, 3 = to a considerable degree, 4 = very much). The official DASS scoring uses 0 to 3, so subtract 1 (and double the DASS-21 sums to compare with DASS-42 norms). No item is reverse-keyed. The items were shown in a random order among the 42, one at a time.

Over half of the respondents connected from Malaysia, so use country when the population matters.

References

Henry, J. D., & Crawford, J. R. (2005). The short-form version of the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21): Construct validity and normative data in a large non-clinical sample. British Journal of Clinical Psychology, 44(2), 227-239. doi:10.1348/014466505X29657

Lovibond, S. H., & Lovibond, P. F. (1995). Manual for the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (2nd ed.). Psychology Foundation.

Osman, A., Wong, J. L., Bagge, C. L., Freedenthal, S., Gutierrez, P. M., & Lozano, G. (2012). The Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21 (DASS-21): Further examination of dimensions, scale reliability, and correlates. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 68(12), 1322-1338. doi:10.1002/jclp.21908

See also

sc_builtin_instrument(), rses_items, mini_ipip_items

Examples

table(dass_items$scale_label)
#> 
#>    Anxiety Depression     Stress 
#>          7          7          7 
# DASS-21 scale sums on the official 0 to 3 scoring
sums <- sapply(split(dass_items$item, dass_items$scale),
               function(i) rowSums(dass_real[i] - 1))
round(cor(sums), 2)
#>      A    D    S
#> A 1.00 0.62 0.75
#> D 0.62 1.00 0.71
#> S 0.75 0.71 1.00
